title: The king's regret
hook: Ajatasattu confesses; the Buddha says had he not killed his father he would have seen the truth that night

segments.voice: Yesterday: veluriya, and your line, the gem and the thread. Did you notice the knowing running through something ordinary? Today the long night in the mango grove ends. Day five hundred thirty-one.

The teaching is over. The Buddha has walked the king all the way from the honored slave to the end of the taints. The lamps are still burning in the pavilion. And King Ajatasattu, who rode out because he wanted peace in his heart, does two things. First he says the familiar words that close these discourses: excellent, as if something overturned had been set upright. He goes for refuge. And then he says what he came carrying. Today: the king's regret.
screen: `THE LAMPS STILL BURNING.` → `EXCELLENT, LIKE SOMETHING SET UPRIGHT.` → `THEN, WHAT HE CAME CARRYING.`

segments.voice: Lord, the king says, a transgression overcame me. Foolish, confused and unskillful as I was, for the sake of the throne, I took the life of my father. A good man, a righteous king. May the Blessed One accept my confession of this, so that I may restrain myself in the future. The Pali word is accaya: a transgression, a going beyond the line. The Buddha's answer is direct. Yes, great king, a transgression overcame you. He doesn't soften the deed. But since you see it as a transgression, and make amends in line with the dhamma, we accept it. For this is growth in the noble discipline: to see a wrong as wrong, make amends, and restrain yourself in the future. The king rises, bows, and leaves. And when he's gone, the Buddha says something to the monks that is hard to hear. This king is wounded, he says, damaged. If he had not taken his father's life, the clear eye of the dhamma would have opened in him tonight, on that very seat. Two things are true at once, and the discourse holds both. Confession is real, and welcomed. It's called growth, not humiliation. And the deed is also real. It has left a mark that one honest night can't remove. The king came for peace of heart and received something more sober: the path is still open to him, but he will walk it carrying what he did. Later tradition remembers Ajatasattu as a supporter of the community. The canon doesn't pretend the night erased the past. It just doesn't close the door.
screen: `I TOOK MY FATHER'S LIFE` · `SEEN AS WRONG, WE ACCEPT IT` · `THIS IS GROWTH IN THE DISCIPLINE` · `HE WOULD HAVE SEEN, BUT FOR THAT` · then, large: `REGRET, CONFESSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit honestly with a regret. Choose a small one, something you can hold without being flooded. Name it plainly to yourself, no excuses and no punishment: I did this. Then notice the three steps from the text. Seeing it as a mistake. Making some amends, if there's a way. And intending to do differently next time. You don't have to fix it in two minutes. Just let it be seen, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Accaya. A transgression, a going beyond the line: the king's wrong, seen as wrong, confessed and accepted as growth, while the deed still leaves its mark. Today's word.
Your line: regret, confessed. Today, if you owe someone a plain apology, offer it without a single excuse attached. Day five hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics confess offenses to one another in regular ceremonies, and lay Buddhists in some traditions acknowledge wrongdoing and renew their precepts, following the pattern in DN 2: seeing a wrong as wrong, making amends, and resolving restraint.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a king who killed his own father confesses it and asks you to accept his confession. what do you say?
options: it was a wrong, and since you see it so and make amends, we accept it.
fork.reveal: the Buddha neither excuses nor rejects. he names the wrong, accepts the confession as growth, and only afterward tells the monks what the deed cost the king.

original.note: Pali accaya: a transgression, literally a going beyond. the word in the king's confession.

trapdoor: what you thought: confession wipes the slate clean.
what it means: in DN 2 confession is accepted as real growth, but the deed still left a mark.

what a scholar hears: the commentary says that, had he not killed his father, the king would have become a stream-enterer that night; later tradition remembers him as patron of the First Council at Rajagaha.
recall: a discourse, often explained as thread

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta, the closing section

notes: DN 2 paraphrased. Confirm the confession wording (foolish, confused, unskillful; for the sake of sovereignty; a righteous man, a righteous king), the Buddha's acceptance formula, and the closing remark (khata / upahata: 'wounded', 'damaged') with 'the dust-free, stainless eye of dhamma would have arisen on this very seat'.
Confirm the traditions in the trapdoor (stream-entry per the commentary; patronage of the First Council).
The practice asks listeners to choose a small regret; keep it gentle.
Editor review: replaced 'what so many listeners say'; Ajatasattu's later support credited to later tradition, not 'the texts'.
